title: Who patches the guest OS on IaaS VMs?
question: Your team runs an application on IaaS virtual machines in a public cloud. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
options: The hypervisor vendor
Your team, the customer
The cloud provider, automatically
Nobody; IaaS images never need patching
explanation: With IaaS the provider secures the physical hosts, network and hypervisor, but everything from the guest OS upward (patches, runtime, app, data) belongs to the customer. Responsibility shifts towards the provider only as you move to PaaS and SaaS, where the provider manages the OS for you.

title: Picking the right service model
question: A small team wants to deploy its own web application code but does not want to provision servers, patch operating systems or manage runtimes. Which service model fits best?
options: Colocation in a data center
Software as a Service (SaaS)
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
explanation: PaaS lets you bring your code while the provider manages the OS, runtime and scaling infrastructure. IaaS would still leave OS and runtime management with the team, SaaS is a finished application you consume rather than one you deploy, and colocation means owning the hardware.

title: Latency spikes after idle periods
question: A serverless function API has p50 latency of 40 ms, but the first request after ~15 minutes of no traffic takes 2-3 seconds. What is the most likely cause and a standard mitigation?
options: DNS caching; lower the TTL on the API's DNS record
A cold start; keep pre-initialized capacity with provisioned concurrency or minimum instances
TLS renegotiation; switch the API from HTTPS to plain HTTP
Database lock contention; add an index on the hot table
explanation: After idling, the platform reclaims execution environments, so the next request pays for creating a new one and running init code (a cold start). Provisioned concurrency (Lambda) or minimum instances (Cloud Run, Functions premium/flex) keep warm environments ready. DNS, locks or TLS would not correlate so cleanly with idle time.

title: Cheap capacity for interruptible jobs
question: A nightly batch job is checkpointed and can be restarted at any time. You want to cut compute cost as much as possible. Which purchasing option fits?
options: Spot instances, which can be reclaimed by the provider at short notice
On-demand instances with no commitment
Dedicated hosts reserved for your account
Bare-metal instances with a three-year reservation
explanation: Spot capacity uses spare provider capacity at a steep discount, with the tradeoff that instances can be interrupted with a short warning. That is acceptable for fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch work. Dedicated hosts and bare-metal reservations cost more, and on-demand is flexible but full price.

title: Users logged out after scale-in
question: A web app behind an autoscaling load balancer stores login sessions in each instance's memory. Users are randomly logged out, mostly when the group scales in or a deploy happens. What is the best fix?
options: Move session state to an external store such as a managed cache or database so instances are stateless
Disable autoscaling so the instance count never changes
Increase each instance's memory so sessions are evicted less often
Lower the load balancer idle timeout so sessions refresh faster
explanation: Instance-local state disappears when an instance is removed, and requests may land on a different instance. Externalising session state makes instances disposable, which is what elastic and container/serverless compute assume. Disabling autoscaling loses elasticity, more memory does not survive termination, and timeouts do not move state.

title: A 40-minute job on AWS Lambda
question: A team wants to move a video transcoding step that runs 30-45 minutes per file to AWS Lambda. What is the key problem?
options: Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes, so the job should run on containers or batch compute (or be split into shorter steps)
Lambda only supports interpreted languages, so FFmpeg cannot be used
Lambda functions are limited to 1 vCPU, so the job would be throttled
Lambda cannot read from S3, so the input files must be moved to EFS first
explanation: A Lambda invocation can run for at most 900 seconds; longer work is killed. Long-running jobs fit ECS/Fargate, AWS Batch or a Step Functions workflow over smaller chunks. Lambda reads S3 natively, supports container images and custom runtimes, and scales vCPU with configured memory beyond a single core.

title: Storing user-uploaded images
question: An app needs to store millions of user-uploaded images that are written once, read often and served via HTTP URLs. Which storage type is the natural fit?
options: The local ephemeral disk of the web servers
Object storage (for example Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage)
A relational database table with a BLOB column
Block storage volumes attached to each web server
explanation: Object storage is designed for large numbers of immutable objects, scales practically without limit, is highly durable and is addressable over HTTP. Block volumes are tied to instances, storing images in a relational DB bloats it and makes it expensive to scale, and ephemeral disks lose data when instances are replaced.

title: Retaining rarely read logs for years
question: Audit logs are read frequently for 30 days, almost never after 90 days, but must be retained for 7 years. Retrieval within 12 hours is acceptable for old logs. What is the most cost-effective approach?
options: A lifecycle policy that transitions objects to infrequent-access and then an archive storage class
Keep everything in the standard storage class and enable versioning
Copy old logs into the primary transactional database
Store old logs on provisioned block volumes that are detached
explanation: Lifecycle rules automatically move objects to cheaper classes as they age; archive classes have very low storage cost in exchange for retrieval delays and fees, which matches the 12-hour tolerance. Standard storage plus versioning costs more, detached volumes still bill provisioned capacity, and a transactional DB is the most expensive place for cold data.

title: Throttling on a date partition key
question: A DynamoDB table of events uses the event date (e.g. 2026-10-05) as its partition key. Writes are heavily throttled even though total consumed capacity is well below table capacity. Why?
options: The table needs a global secondary index before it can accept writes
On-demand tables throttle any request larger than 1 KB
DynamoDB cannot store more than one item per partition key value
All of today's writes target one partition key, creating a hot partition that exceeds per-partition throughput
explanation: Throughput is distributed across partitions by partition key, and each partition has its own limits. A low-cardinality key that concentrates current traffic (like today's date) sends all writes to one partition. Using a high-cardinality key or write sharding (e.g. date#random-suffix) spreads the load. Items can share a partition key via sort keys, and GSIs or item size are not the cause here.

title: Inbound allowed, responses blocked
question: In a VPC, a subnet's network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 from anywhere, and the instance's security group also allows inbound 443. Clients still time out. The NACL's outbound rules only allow port 443. What is wrong?
options: Security groups are stateless and need an explicit outbound rule for port 443
NACLs can only be applied to load balancers, not subnets
NACLs are stateless, so outbound rules must also allow responses to the clients' ephemeral ports
Port 443 requires a NAT gateway to accept inbound connections
explanation: Network ACLs evaluate each direction independently, so return traffic to the client's ephemeral port range (e.g. 1024-65535) must be explicitly allowed outbound. Security groups are stateful and automatically allow return traffic. NACLs are subnet-level, and NAT gateways are for outbound-initiated traffic, not inbound.

title: Routing /api and /static differently
question: You need one public endpoint that sends /api/* requests to one service and /static/* to another, based on the HTTP path. Which load balancer type do you need?
options: A NAT gateway
A layer 7 (application) load balancer
A DNS round-robin record
A layer 4 (network) load balancer
explanation: Path-based routing requires inspecting HTTP requests, which is what layer 7 load balancers such as AWS ALB do. A layer 4 balancer only sees IPs, ports and protocols, DNS round-robin cannot see paths, and a NAT gateway provides outbound connectivity rather than load balancing.

title: Huge NAT bill from S3 traffic
question: Instances in private subnets read terabytes per day from S3 in the same region through a NAT gateway, and NAT data-processing charges dominate the bill. What is the simplest fix?
options: Move the instances to public subnets and attach Elastic IPs
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and route table entries so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateway
Replace the NAT gateway with a larger instance type
explanation: A gateway endpoint for S3 adds a route that keeps S3 traffic on the AWS network without passing through the NAT gateway, and gateway endpoints carry no additional charge. Moving instances to public subnets weakens security, NAT size does not change per-GB processing charges, and Transfer Acceleration targets long-distance client uploads.

title: Autoscaling to a utilization target
question: You want an Auto Scaling group to add or remove instances automatically to keep average CPU around 50%, without writing step thresholds by hand. Which policy type fits?
options: Target tracking scaling
Simple scaling with a single alarm
Manual desired-capacity changes
Scheduled scaling
explanation: Target tracking works like a thermostat: you pick a metric and target value, and the service creates and manages the alarms and adjustments to keep the metric near it. Scheduled scaling only reacts to time, manual changes do not react at all, and simple scaling requires you to define thresholds and fixed adjustments yourself.

title: Access keys in an EC2 config file
question: An application on EC2 reads AWS access keys from a config file to call S3 and SQS. What is the recommended replacement?
options: Create a separate IAM user per instance with its own long-lived keys
Embed the keys in the AMI so they never appear in source control
Attach an IAM role via an instance profile so the SDK obtains temporary, auto-rotated credentials
Store the same access keys in an environment variable instead
explanation: IAM roles for EC2 deliver short-lived credentials through the instance metadata service and rotate them automatically, removing long-lived secrets entirely. Moving keys to environment variables or the AMI still leaves static credentials that can leak, and per-instance IAM users multiply the problem.

title: Allow and deny on the same action
question: A user's identity policy allows s3:DeleteObject on a bucket, but an attached permissions boundary or SCP has an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteObject. What happens when the user deletes an object?
options: The request is allowed, because identity policies take precedence
The most recently attached policy wins
The request is allowed only if MFA was used
The request is denied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow
explanation: AWS policy evaluation starts from an implicit deny, an allow is required to grant access, and any applicable explicit Deny always wins. Order of attachment and policy type do not let an allow override it, and MFA only matters if a policy condition references it.

title: Outages during DB password rotation
question: After enabling automatic database password rotation, an app fails for a few minutes on each rotation: it reads the secret once at startup and keeps using it. Which change best removes the outage?
options: Disable rotation and lengthen the password to compensate
Re-fetch the secret on authentication failure (or cache with a short TTL) and use an alternating-users rotation so the old credential stays valid
Restart all instances manually right before every rotation
Store the password in the container image so it is always available
explanation: Rotation changes the credential under a running app, so clients must refresh it; an alternating-users strategy keeps the previous user's credentials valid during the switch so in-flight clients keep working. Disabling rotation trades away security, manual restarts are fragile, and baking secrets into images is both insecure and still stale after rotation.

title: What RPO measures
question: A business states an RPO of 15 minutes for its order database. What does that mean?
options: At most 15 minutes of data may be lost, measured back from the moment of failure
The system must be back online within 15 minutes of an outage
Backups must be retained for at least 15 minutes
Failover must be tested every 15 minutes
explanation: Recovery Point Objective is the maximum acceptable data loss expressed as time since the last recoverable point. The time to restore service is the Recovery Time Objective (RTO). Retention and test frequency are separate concerns.

title: Choosing a DR strategy
question: A workload needs RTO of a few minutes and RPO of seconds after a regional outage, but the business will not pay for full active/active capacity in two regions. Which DR strategy fits best?
options: Multi-site active/active at full capacity in both regions
Backup and restore from daily snapshots copied to the second region
Pilot light with only data replicated and infrastructure created at failover time
Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully functional copy running in the second region with continuous replication
explanation: Warm standby keeps a running, smaller environment that can take traffic immediately and scale up, giving RTO in minutes with replicated data for seconds of RPO. Backup and restore gives hours of RTO and RPO, pilot light needs time to provision and start services, and active/active meets the goals but is the expensive option ruled out.

title: What multi-AZ does and does not cover
question: An app runs across three availability zones in one region with a zone-redundant database. Which event is this design NOT designed to survive?
options: A network partition isolating one zone
Loss of a single host running one app instance
A power failure in one zone's data center
A region-wide outage affecting all zones
explanation: Availability zones are physically separate data centers with independent power, cooling and networking within one region, so spreading across them tolerates host and zone failures. Surviving a whole-region outage requires a multi-region design with a defined failover process.

title: Data loss after cross-region failover
question: The primary database replicates asynchronously to another region with typical lag of 5 seconds. The primary region fails and you fail over. What should you expect?
options: The replica is unusable until the primary region recovers
Transactions committed in the last seconds before the failure may be lost, so RPO is greater than zero
Failover is impossible without synchronous replication
No data loss, because asynchronous replication confirms every commit in both regions
explanation: With asynchronous replication the primary acknowledges commits before they reach the replica, so anything inside the lag window is lost on failover. Synchronous cross-region replication would avoid that but adds write latency. The replica can still be promoted; you are trading a small RPO for performance.

title: A bad DELETE replicated everywhere
question: A buggy migration ran DELETE without a WHERE clause on the primary database. The multi-region replicas and zone-redundant standby all show the same missing rows within seconds. What should the DR plan have included?
options: More replicas in additional regions to raise availability
Point-in-time restore from backups (ideally isolated/immutable), because replication faithfully copies logical corruption
Shorter DNS TTLs so traffic could fail over faster
A synchronous replica, which would have rejected the destructive statement
explanation: Replication and HA protect against infrastructure failures, not bad writes: a valid DELETE is replicated like any other change. Recovery needs backups with point-in-time restore to before the incident, and immutable or isolated copies also protect against ransomware. Synchronous replicas, more regions or faster DNS failover would all contain the same deleted data.

title: The four golden signals
question: According to Google's SRE guidance, which set makes up the four golden signals for monitoring a user-facing system?
options: Uptime, throughput, cost, headcount
CPU, memory, disk, network
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation
Logs, metrics, traces, profiles
explanation: The SRE book recommends latency, traffic, errors and saturation as the minimum set to monitor for user-facing systems because they describe what users experience and how close the system is to its limits. Host resource metrics are useful causes, not symptoms, and logs/metrics/traces are telemetry types rather than signals.

title: Paging on CPU vs error budget
question: An on-call team is paged whenever CPU exceeds 80%, yet most pages need no action and a recent outage with low CPU was missed. What alerting approach does SRE practice recommend instead?
options: Lower the CPU threshold to 60% so problems are caught earlier
Page on every ERROR log line from any service
Remove paging and rely on a daily dashboard review
Alert on SLO error-budget burn rate (e.g. multi-window burn-rate alerts) based on user-visible symptoms
explanation: Burn-rate alerts fire when users are actually being hurt fast enough to threaten the SLO, which improves precision and recall versus resource thresholds. A lower CPU threshold creates more noise, paging on every error line is unmanageable, and dashboards alone miss urgent incidents.

title: SQS messages processed twice
question: Workers take about 2 minutes to process each SQS message, and the queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. Many messages are processed twice. What is happening?
options: Long polling is causing workers to read the same message simultaneously
SQS standard queues always deliver every message exactly twice
The dead-letter queue is redriving messages back to the source queue
The message becomes visible again before processing finishes, so another worker receives it
explanation: While a consumer processes a message it is hidden for the visibility timeout; if it is not deleted in time it reappears and another consumer gets it. Set the timeout above the processing time (or extend it while working) and keep handlers idempotent, since standard queues are at-least-once anyway. Long polling and DLQs do not cause this pattern.

title: Ordering per customer in SQS
question: Account events must be processed in order per customer, but different customers can be processed in parallel. How do you get this with SQS?
options: Use a standard queue with a single consumer thread
Use a FIFO queue with one fixed message group ID for all messages
Use a FIFO queue and set the message group ID to the customer ID
Use a standard queue and sort messages by timestamp in the consumer
explanation: FIFO queues preserve order within a message group and allow different groups to be processed in parallel, matching per-customer ordering. A standard queue offers best-effort ordering only, client-side sorting cannot fix gaps, and a single group serializes all customers.

title: Read replica vs Multi-AZ
question: A team added an RDS read replica in another AZ, expecting it to provide automatic failover if the primary instance fails. What is the flaw?
options: Read replicas use asynchronous replication for read scaling; automatic failover comes from a Multi-AZ deployment's synchronously replicated standby
Read replicas cannot be placed in a different AZ from the primary
Multi-AZ standbys are only available for Aurora, not RDS
Automatic failover requires two read replicas in different regions
explanation: RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby and fails over automatically, typically keeping the same endpoint. Read replicas replicate asynchronously and must be promoted (losing in-flight writes) - they exist mainly to offload reads. Replicas can be in other AZs or regions, and Multi-AZ is available for standard RDS engines.

title: One poison message retries the whole batch
question: A Lambda function consumes SQS in batches of 10. One malformed message makes the function throw, so all 10 messages return to the queue and are reprocessed repeatedly. What is the best fix?
options: Set the batch size to 10,000 so failures are diluted
Catch the exception and return success so the batch is deleted
Set the visibility timeout to zero so retries happen immediately
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures and return only the failed message IDs, plus configure a dead-letter queue via redrive policy
explanation: With partial batch responses, Lambda deletes the successful messages and only the reported failures become visible again; a redrive policy moves repeatedly failing messages to a DLQ. Swallowing errors silently loses data, larger batches increase blast radius, and zero visibility timeout causes immediate duplicate processing.

title: Account-wide guardrail against public buckets
question: Security wants to make sure no S3 bucket in an account can be made public through ACLs or bucket policies, even by mistake. Which feature provides this guardrail?
options: S3 Block Public Access at the account level
S3 Transfer Acceleration
S3 Versioning
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
explanation: Block Public Access settings override ACLs and bucket policies that would grant public access, and setting them at the account level covers existing and future buckets. Versioning protects against overwrites, Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads, and Intelligent-Tiering optimises storage cost.

title: Google Cloud resource hierarchy
question: In Google Cloud, an IAM role granted on a folder applies to which resources?
options: Only resources created after the grant
Only the folder object itself, not its projects
All projects and resources beneath that folder, through policy inheritance
All projects in the organization, regardless of folder
explanation: Google Cloud's hierarchy is organization > folders > projects > resources, and allow policies are inherited downward, so a grant on a folder applies to everything below it. It does not reach sibling folders, and inheritance covers existing and new resources alike.

title: CI deploys without service account keys
question: A GitHub Actions pipeline deploys to Google Cloud using a downloaded service account JSON key stored as a repository secret. What is the recommended keyless alternative?
options: Rotate the JSON key weekly and keep it in the repository secret
Create a user account for the pipeline and store its password
Workload Identity Federation, exchanging the CI provider's OIDC token for short-lived Google credentials
Grant the Owner role to allUsers on the deployment project
explanation: Workload Identity Federation trusts an external identity provider's tokens (such as GitHub's OIDC) and issues short-lived credentials, eliminating long-lived keys that can leak. Rotating keys reduces but does not remove that risk, user accounts are not meant for workloads, and granting roles to allUsers is a severe security hole.

title: Non-thread-safe code on Cloud Run
question: A legacy service moved to Cloud Run starts producing corrupted responses under load, though it worked fine with one request at a time. The code uses global mutable state. Which setting is most relevant?
options: Minimum instances, which defaults to 80 and should be set to 0
The request timeout, which must be raised to 60 minutes
Maximum concurrent requests per instance, which defaults to 80; set it to 1 for code that is not thread-safe
CPU always-allocated billing, which disables multithreading
explanation: Unlike classic FaaS, a Cloud Run instance serves many requests at once (default concurrency 80), so shared global state can be corrupted. Setting concurrency to 1 restores one-request-per-instance semantics at the cost of more instances; the better long-term fix is removing shared mutable state. Min instances, timeouts and billing mode do not change concurrency.

title: Ordered delivery in Pub/Sub
question: A publisher sets an ordering key per account on Pub/Sub messages, but subscribers still see out-of-order events for the same account. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: Ordering requires a dead-letter topic to be configured
Message ordering was not enabled on the subscription
The topic needs exactly one partition per ordering key
Ordering keys only work with push subscriptions
explanation: Pub/Sub only delivers messages with the same ordering key in order when the subscription has message ordering enabled; publishing with keys alone is not enough. Ordering works with pull and push, Pub/Sub topics have no user-managed partitions, and dead-letter topics are unrelated.

title: Event-driven containers that scale to zero
question: A team has a dozen containerized microservices that consume Service Bus queues and should scale to zero when idle. They want KEDA-style scaling and Dapr but do not want to operate Kubernetes. Which Azure service fits best?
options: Azure Container Apps
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Kubernetes Service
Azure App Service on a Premium plan
explanation: Container Apps is a serverless container platform built on Kubernetes, KEDA and Dapr, with event-driven scaling including scale to zero and no cluster to manage. AKS offers the same building blocks but you operate the cluster, App Service is optimised for web apps rather than queue-driven scale to zero, and VM scale sets are IaaS.

title: When you need AKS
question: A platform team must install custom operators with CRDs, run DaemonSets for a security agent and use kubectl directly against the cluster. Which Azure compute option supports this?
options: Azure App Service for Containers
Azure Container Apps
Azure Functions Flex Consumption
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
explanation: AKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane with full access to the Kubernetes API, so CRDs, operators and DaemonSets work. Container Apps deliberately hides the Kubernetes API, and Functions and App Service are higher-level PaaS options without cluster-level access.

title: Zero-downtime deploys on App Service
question: You want to deploy a new version of an App Service web app, warm it up, test it, and then switch production traffic with an easy rollback. Which feature is designed for this?
options: Scaling out to more instances
Turning on Always On
Deployment slots with swap
Restarting the app after each deploy
explanation: Deployment slots are live apps with their own hostnames; you deploy to staging, warm and validate it, then swap with production, and swap back to roll back. Scaling out and Always On do not isolate a new version, and restarting causes downtime.

title: Stateful fan-out/fan-in in Functions
question: A Functions app must process 5,000 documents in parallel, wait for all of them, then aggregate the results; the workflow may take hours and must survive host restarts. What is the idiomatic approach?
options: A timer-triggered function that polls a static variable for completion
A single HTTP-triggered function that loops over all documents
Durable Functions orchestration using the fan-out/fan-in pattern
Storing progress in each function instance's local temp folder
explanation: Durable Functions orchestrators checkpoint their state to storage, can start many activity functions in parallel, await them all and resume after restarts. A single long HTTP function hits timeouts, static variables and local temp files do not survive scale-out or restarts.

title: Hosting a standard web app
question: An existing ASP.NET Core web app needs managed TLS, custom domains, autoscale and easy CI/CD, with no containers or orchestration skills on the team. Which service is the most straightforward choice?
options: Azure App Service
Azure Batch
Azure Kubernetes Service
Azure Virtual Machines
explanation: App Service is a fully managed PaaS for web apps and APIs with built-in TLS, custom domains, autoscale and deployment integrations, and it runs code without requiring containers. AKS and VMs add operational overhead, and Azure Batch is for large-scale parallel jobs.

title: Storage redundancy for zone and region failure
question: A storage account must survive the loss of an availability zone with no data loss for synchronous writes and also keep a copy in a secondary region for regional disasters. Which redundancy option fits?
options: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
explanation: GZRS replicates synchronously across three zones in the primary region and asynchronously to a secondary region. ZRS lacks a secondary region, GRS uses LRS (single data center) in the primary region, and LRS protects only against hardware failures within one data center.

title: Reading an archived blob
question: A blob in the Archive access tier must be read by an application today. What must happen first?
options: The storage account must be converted to premium performance
Nothing; Archive blobs can be read directly at a higher price
The blob must be rehydrated to an online tier (Hot, Cool or Cold), which can take hours
The blob must be copied to a file share before reading
explanation: The Archive tier is offline: data cannot be read until the blob is rehydrated to an online tier, either by changing its tier or copying it, which may take up to many hours depending on priority. Premium accounts and file shares are unrelated to rehydration.

title: Keeping connection strings after geo-failover
question: An Azure SQL Database uses active geo-replication. After a regional failover, every app had to be reconfigured with the new server name. Which feature avoids this?
options: Enabling the serverless compute tier with auto-pause
Increasing the database's backup retention period
Failover groups, which expose read-write and read-only listener endpoints that follow the primary
Zone-redundant configuration on the primary database
explanation: Failover groups wrap geo-replication with stable DNS listener endpoints that redirect to the current primary after failover, so connection strings do not change. Zone redundancy protects within a region, backup retention affects restores, and serverless affects compute billing.

title: Too many PostgreSQL connections
question: A serverless app creates many short-lived connections to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server and hits connection limits and high CPU from connection churn. What built-in option helps most?
options: Enable the built-in PgBouncer connection pooler and connect through it (port 6432)
Switch the server to the burstable compute tier
Disable SSL so connection setup is cheaper
Increase max_connections far above the server's memory capacity
explanation: Flexible server includes PgBouncer, which multiplexes many client connections onto a smaller pool of server connections; clients connect to port 6432 on the same host. Raising max_connections beyond memory causes instability, a burstable tier reduces capacity, and disabling TLS is insecure.

title: Removing a storage connection string
question: An App Service app reads blobs using a storage account connection string with the account key in app settings. What is the recommended way to remove that secret?
options: Move the connection string into a Git-ignored local file
Enable a managed identity, grant it a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader, and authenticate with DefaultAzureCredential
Grant the app the Owner role on the storage account and keep the key
Use a SAS token with no expiry date in app settings
explanation: Managed identities let the app obtain Microsoft Entra tokens without any stored secret, and data-plane RBAC roles grant just the blob access needed. Local files and non-expiring SAS tokens are still long-lived secrets, and Owner is a management-plane role that is far too broad.

title: System- vs user-assigned identity
question: Eight Container Apps must use the same identity to access a Key Vault, and the identity's role assignments must persist even when individual apps are deleted and recreated. Which option fits?
options: The developers' own Entra user accounts
A system-assigned managed identity on each app
A user-assigned managed identity attached to all eight apps
A service principal with a client secret in each app's settings
explanation: A user-assigned identity is a standalone Azure resource with its own lifecycle that can be shared by many resources, so role assignments survive app redeployments. System-assigned identities are tied to one resource and deleted with it, client secrets reintroduce credentials, and personal accounts must not be used by workloads.

title: Key Vault secrets in app settings
question: How can an App Service app consume a secret from Key Vault as a normal app setting without changing application code?
options: Enable public network access on the vault so the app can read it anonymously
Mount the Key Vault as a network drive on the app
Copy the secret value into the app setting during each deployment
Use a Key Vault reference such as @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) resolved via the app's managed identity
explanation: Key Vault references let App Service resolve app settings from Key Vault at runtime using the app's managed identity, so code reads an ordinary environment variable. Copying values loses central rotation, vaults cannot be mounted as drives, and Key Vault never allows anonymous secret reads.

title: 403 reading a secret with Key Vault Reader
question: A managed identity has the 'Key Vault Reader' role on an RBAC-enabled vault, yet GET on a secret returns 403 Forbidden. What is the fix?
options: Grant 'Reader' on the resource group, which includes data-plane access
Wait 24 hours for role assignments to propagate
Assign 'Key Vault Secrets User', because Key Vault Reader can read metadata but not secret values
Add an access policy, since RBAC vaults still evaluate access policies first
explanation: Key Vault Reader is limited to metadata; reading secret contents is a data-plane action granted by roles like Key Vault Secrets User. Role propagation usually takes minutes, not a day. With the RBAC permission model, access policies are not evaluated, and the generic Reader role covers only the management plane.

title: High-volume telemetry ingestion
question: Millions of IoT devices send telemetry that must be ingested at very high throughput, retained for a few days and processed by several independent stream-processing consumers. Which Azure service fits best?
options: Azure Event Grid
Azure Event Hubs
Azure Queue Storage
Azure Service Bus queues
explanation: Event Hubs is a partitioned, high-throughput event streaming platform with retention and independent consumer groups, similar to Kafka. Service Bus is for transactional business messaging, Event Grid routes discrete events to handlers rather than retaining streams, and Queue Storage lacks streaming semantics and multiple consumer groups.

title: Ordered, reliable order processing
question: Order commands must be processed reliably with dead-lettering and duplicate detection, and all commands for the same order must be handled in sequence by one consumer at a time. Which design fits?
options: Event Hubs with a single consumer group and checkpointing
Event Grid custom topic with a webhook subscriber
Blob Storage with change feed processing
Service Bus queue with sessions, using the order ID as the session ID
explanation: Service Bus provides enterprise messaging features (DLQ, duplicate detection, transactions), and sessions guarantee FIFO, exclusive processing per session ID. Event Grid offers no ordering guarantees, Event Hubs provides partition ordering but not per-message settlement and DLQs, and the blob change feed is not a command queue.

title: Reacting to new blobs
question: You want a function to run whenever a new blob is uploaded to a storage account, with push-based delivery and no polling. Which service is designed for this?
options: Azure Data Factory
Azure Event Grid
Azure Service Bus
Azure Event Hubs
explanation: Event Grid is a push-based event routing service that natively publishes Blob Storage events like BlobCreated to subscribers such as Functions. Event Hubs is for high-volume streams, Service Bus is for application messages your code sends, and Data Factory is a data integration tool.

title: Messages land in the DLQ despite success
question: A Service Bus consumer uses peek-lock with a 30-second lock duration. Handlers take about 90 seconds. Messages are redelivered repeatedly and end up in the dead-letter queue with MaxDeliveryCountExceeded. What is the cause?
options: The dead-letter queue is full and is pushing messages back
Sessions are disabled, which makes every message expire after 30 seconds
Peek-lock deletes the message on receipt, so retries come from the sender
The lock expires before the handler completes, so completion fails and each redelivery increments the delivery count
explanation: In peek-lock mode the message is locked for the lock duration; if it is not settled in time the lock is lost, the message becomes available again and its delivery count increases until it hits MaxDeliveryCount and is dead-lettered. Fix it by renewing locks (SDK auto-lock-renewal) or increasing the lock duration. Receive-and-delete is the mode that removes messages on receipt.

title: Duplicates despite duplicate detection
question: A queue has duplicate detection enabled and senders set MessageId to the business ID. The team still sees an order processed twice after a consumer crashed right after writing to the database but before completing the message. Why?
options: Duplicate detection only drops duplicate sends within its window; delivery is still at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent
The lock duration resets the duplicate detection window to zero
MessageId must be a GUID generated by the SDK for detection to apply
Duplicate detection requires partitioning to be disabled to work at all
explanation: Duplicate detection prevents the same MessageId from being accepted twice by the queue, which handles sender retries. It cannot stop redelivery of the same message when the consumer fails to settle it, so side effects must be idempotent (e.g. upsert keyed on order ID or an inbox table). Any stable application-controlled MessageId works, which is the point of the feature.

title: Global vs regional layer 7
question: A web app is deployed in East US and West Europe. You need a single global entry point with WAF, edge TLS termination, caching and automatic failover between regions. Which service fits?
options: Azure Load Balancer
Azure Application Gateway
Azure Front Door
Azure VPN Gateway
explanation: Front Door is a global layer 7 entry point on Microsoft's edge with WAF, caching and health-probe-based failover across regions. Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer, Load Balancer is regional layer 4, and VPN Gateway connects networks rather than serving public web traffic.

title: Private endpoint still resolves public IP
question: You created a private endpoint for an Azure SQL server and disabled public network access. The app in a peered VNet now fails because myserver.database.windows.net still resolves to a public IP. What is missing?
options: A privatelink.database.windows.net private DNS zone with the endpoint's record, linked to the app's VNet
An NSG rule allowing outbound port 1433 to the Internet service tag
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Sql on the database server
A public IP address attached to the private endpoint
explanation: Private endpoints rely on DNS: the public name must resolve via a CNAME to the privatelink zone, which needs a private DNS zone (or custom DNS) linked to every VNet that resolves it. Opening outbound Internet does not help when public access is disabled, private endpoints have no public IPs, and service endpoints are a different mechanism.

title: Balancing TCP traffic to VMs
question: You need to distribute TCP traffic for a non-HTTP game server across VMs in one region with very low latency. Which Azure service is designed for this?
options: Azure Load Balancer
Azure Application Gateway
Azure API Management
Azure Front Door
explanation: Azure Load Balancer operates at layer 4 for TCP and UDP within a region with high throughput and low latency. Front Door and Application Gateway are HTTP(S) layer 7 services, and API Management is an API gateway for HTTP APIs.

title: Querying collected logs
question: Where do you write KQL queries to analyse logs collected by Azure Monitor and Application Insights (workspace-based)?
options: Azure Advisor
Azure Resource Graph Explorer only
The storage account's blob container browser
Log Analytics in an Azure Monitor Logs workspace
explanation: Azure Monitor Logs stores data in Log Analytics workspaces, queried with Kusto Query Language through Log Analytics. Advisor gives recommendations, Resource Graph queries resource metadata, and a blob browser cannot query telemetry.

title: Cutting Application Insights cost
question: A high-traffic API's Application Insights ingestion costs are too high. You enable sampling. Why can you still trust request counts and follow complete traces for sampled operations?
options: Sampling only discards exceptions, leaving all requests intact
Sampled-out telemetry is stored in a cheaper tier and merged at query time
Sampling compresses telemetry without dropping any items
Sampling decisions are made per operation/trace ID, and retained items carry a weight so aggregates are statistically adjusted
explanation: Application Insights sampling keeps or drops whole operations together based on the trace ID, so related requests, dependencies and logs stay correlated, and each retained item represents several items so metrics are scaled. It does drop data permanently and does not target exceptions only.

title: Near-real-time alert on error rate
question: You want to be notified within about a minute when an App Service's HTTP 5xx count exceeds a threshold over a 5-minute window, and you want to avoid the cost of log queries. Which alert type fits?
options: A log search alert running every 24 hours
A metric alert rule on the platform Http5xx metric
A Service Health alert
An activity log alert on resource writes
explanation: Metric alerts evaluate platform metrics frequently with low latency and no log query cost, making them ideal for threshold conditions like 5xx counts. Log search alerts are for complex queries, activity log alerts fire on control-plane events, and Service Health alerts report Azure platform incidents.

title: What makes a pipeline ELT
question: What distinguishes ELT from ETL?
options: Raw data is loaded into the target system first and transformed there using its compute
ELT never transforms data; it only replicates source tables
ELT runs only as streaming, while ETL runs only as batch
Data is transformed on a separate server before being loaded
explanation: In ELT, extracted data is loaded raw into a warehouse or lakehouse and transformed in place, leveraging scalable target compute and keeping raw history. ETL transforms on an intermediate engine before loading. Both transform data and both can be batch or near-real-time.

title: Reruns duplicate rows
question: A daily job appends yesterday's sales to a table. When it is retried after a partial failure, rows are duplicated. What design change makes reruns safe?
options: Make the load idempotent, e.g. overwrite the day's partition or MERGE/upsert on a business key
Run the job twice and deduplicate weekly
Increase the job's timeout so it never fails partway
Add a retry limit of one so the job never runs twice
explanation: Idempotent tasks produce the same result no matter how many times they run for a given interval, typically by replacing the partition for that interval or upserting on keys. Limiting retries reduces reliability, weekly dedup leaves bad data in between, and longer timeouts do not prevent all failures.

title: Incremental loads that miss deletes
question: An incremental pipeline extracts rows WHERE updated_at > last_run. Analysts find that records deleted in the source still exist in the warehouse, and some rapid updates are missed. What approach addresses both?
options: Switching the warehouse table to a columnar format
Running the timestamp-based query more frequently
Log-based change data capture that reads inserts, updates and deletes from the database's transaction log
Adding an index on updated_at in the source database
explanation: Timestamp queries cannot see hard deletes and depend on applications setting updated_at correctly. Log-based CDC (e.g. Debezium) streams every committed change, including deletes, in order. Running more often or indexing only makes the flawed query faster, and storage format does not change what is extracted.

title: Counting mobile events per hour
question: Mobile apps buffer events offline and upload them hours later. You need accurate counts of user actions per hour in which they happened. Which time should windows be based on?
options: Ingestion time, when the broker received the event
Processing time, when the stream processor handles the event
Event time, the timestamp when the action occurred on the device
Wall-clock time of the dashboard query
explanation: Event time reflects when something actually happened, so windows stay correct even when data arrives late or out of order. Processing and ingestion time would put buffered events into the upload hour, skewing results. Event time requires handling late data, usually with watermarks.

title: Late events and watermarks
question: A Spark Structured Streaming job aggregates 5-minute event-time windows with withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes"). An event arrives 40 minutes after the latest event time seen. What happens?
options: It is older than the watermark, so it may be dropped and not counted in its window
The query fails with a late-data exception
It is always added to its window and the result is re-emitted
It is assigned to the current window instead of its own
explanation: The watermark (max event time seen minus 10 minutes) tells the engine how long to keep window state for late data; data older than that is not guaranteed to be aggregated and is typically dropped, which bounds state. Spark does not fail on late data or reassign it to another window.

title: Streaming dedup state grows forever
question: A streaming job calls dropDuplicates("eventId") on a stream of events without a watermark. Over weeks, state store size and checkpoint times grow until the job becomes unstable. What is the fix?
options: Switch the output mode from append to complete
Add a watermark and include the event-time column (or use a bounded dedup variant) so old keys can be evicted from state
Repartition the stream into a single partition
Increase the trigger interval so fewer micro-batches run
explanation: Without a watermark the engine must remember every eventId forever to detect duplicates, so state grows unbounded. A watermark lets it discard keys older than the threshold, accepting that very late duplicates are not caught. Trigger intervals, complete mode or a single partition do not bound the state and some make it worse.

title: Exactly-once and external side effects
question: A Flink job with checkpointing and exactly-once mode calls an external payment HTTP API for each event. After a failure and restore, some customers are charged twice. Why?
options: Checkpoints are only taken when the job shuts down cleanly
Exactly-once covers the engine's state and transactional sinks; replayed records re-trigger non-idempotent external calls
Exactly-once is disabled automatically whenever parallelism is greater than 1
The HTTP client retried because exactly-once requires UDP
explanation: On recovery the engine rewinds to the last checkpoint and replays input, which is consistent for internal state and for sinks that participate in two-phase commit. Calls to external systems made since the checkpoint happen again, so they need idempotency keys or a transactional/outbox pattern. Parallelism does not disable the guarantee, and checkpoints are taken periodically.

title: When streaming is worth it
question: Which requirement most clearly justifies a streaming pipeline instead of a nightly batch job?
options: Rebuilding a dimension table once a day
Flagging fraudulent card transactions within seconds of them occurring
Archiving last year's logs to cold storage
Producing a monthly finance report for the board
explanation: Streaming adds operational complexity, so it pays off when results must be available with low latency, as in fraud detection. Monthly reports, daily dimension rebuilds and archiving are naturally batch workloads where hours of latency are fine.

title: Warehouse or data lake
question: Data scientists want to keep raw JSON clickstream, images and CSV extracts cheaply for future, not-yet-defined analyses. Which storage architecture fits that need best?
options: An in-memory cache cluster
A data lake on object storage that stores raw data in native formats
An OLTP database tuned for transactions
A relational data warehouse with a fixed star schema
explanation: Data lakes store large volumes of raw structured, semi-structured and unstructured data at low cost with schema-on-read, ideal for exploratory and ML use. A warehouse is best for curated, structured data for BI with schema-on-write, while OLTP databases and caches are not designed for cheap bulk analytical storage.

title: Readers see half-written data
question: Several Spark jobs write Parquet files directly into the same lake folders while BI queries read them. Readers sometimes see partial results and failed jobs leave orphaned files. What addresses this?
options: Adopt an open table format with a transaction log (Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg) for ACID commits and snapshot isolation
Schedule all readers to run only at night
Increase the object storage account's throughput limits
Switch the files from Parquet to CSV
explanation: Table formats such as Delta Lake and Iceberg add a transaction log or metadata layer so writes commit atomically, readers see consistent snapshots, and uncommitted files are ignored - the basis of a lakehouse. The file format inside does not provide transactions, scheduling only hides the issue, and throughput is unrelated to consistency.

title: Historical attributes in a dimension
question: Sales reports must show each order with the customer's region at the time of the order, even after customers move. How should the customer dimension be modelled?
options: Type 1: overwrite the region in place whenever it changes
Slowly changing dimension Type 2: add a new row with effective dates for each change and link facts to the surrogate key
Drop the dimension and store the region on every fact row as free text
Store region only in the source OLTP database and join live
explanation: SCD Type 2 preserves history by versioning dimension rows with validity ranges and surrogate keys, so facts point to the version valid at the time. Type 1 overwrites history, live joins to OLTP show current values and burden production, and free text on facts loses consistency.

title: Ordering guarantees in Kafka
question: Events for each bank account must be consumed in the order they were produced. How do you get this with a multi-partition Kafka topic?
options: Set the topic to use a single consumer group
Enable log compaction on the topic
Kafka guarantees global ordering across all partitions of a topic
Use the account ID as the message key so all its events go to the same partition
explanation: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition, and the default partitioner maps the same key to the same partition. There is no ordering across partitions, consumer groups affect how partitions are shared, and compaction controls retention by key rather than ordering.

title: More consumers than partitions
question: A topic has 6 partitions. To increase throughput, the team runs 10 consumer instances in the same consumer group. What happens?
options: Only 6 consumers receive partitions; the other 4 sit idle as standby
Each partition is split across consumers so all 10 share the load
All 10 consumers receive every message
The group fails to start until consumers equal partitions
explanation: Within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so parallelism is capped by partition count; extra consumers stay idle until a rebalance assigns them work. Receiving every message would require separate consumer groups. To scale further, increase partitions.

title: acks=all with brokers down
question: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2; producers use acks=all. Two of the three replicas for a partition go offline. What happens to writes to that partition?
options: Writes are buffered on the broker until replicas return
Kafka automatically lowers the replication factor to 1
Writes succeed with only the leader, and replicas catch up later
Producers receive NotEnoughReplicas errors, sacrificing availability to avoid acknowledged writes on a single copy
explanation: With acks=all, the leader only acknowledges when at least min.insync.replicas replicas are in sync; with just one remaining the write is rejected. This combination prevents data loss from acknowledging writes held by a single broker. Kafka never silently changes replication factor, and brokers do not buffer rejected writes.

title: Consumers see aborted transactional data
question: A producer uses Kafka transactions to write to two topics atomically. Downstream consumers sometimes process records from transactions that were later aborted. What is the likely cause?
options: Consumers use the default isolation.level=read_uncommitted; they must set read_committed
Transactions only work when both topics have one partition
Transactions require acks=1 on the producer
Aborted records are only filtered when the topic is compacted
explanation: Transactional producers still write records to the log; markers indicate commit or abort. Consumers must use isolation.level=read_committed to see only committed data, while the default read_uncommitted returns everything. Transactions require idempotence and acks=all, and work across multiple partitions and topics.

title: Adding partitions to a keyed topic
question: A keyed topic that relies on per-key ordering is increased from 12 to 24 partitions. What risk should the team expect?
options: The topic becomes read-only until a full rebalance completes
Consumers lose their committed offsets on all partitions
New records for many keys hash to different partitions, so per-key ordering across the change is broken and stateful consumers may see keys move
Existing records are automatically rehashed into the new partitions
explanation: Kafka never moves existing data when partitions are added, but the key-to-partition mapping (hash modulo partition count) changes for new records, so a key's old and new events can live in different partitions. Plan partition counts up front for keyed topics. The topic stays writable and committed offsets for existing partitions remain.

title: Keeping the latest value per key
question: A topic stores customer profile updates keyed by customer ID. New services need to rebuild the current state of all customers without keeping every historical update forever. Which topic setting fits?
options: retention.ms=-1 with cleanup.policy=delete
A replication factor of 1 to reduce storage
A larger segment.bytes so fewer files are kept
cleanup.policy=compact, so Kafka retains at least the latest record for each key
explanation: Log compaction removes older records for a key while keeping the most recent value, so a consumer can rebuild current state from the topic. Infinite delete-based retention keeps every update, replication factor affects durability rather than retention, and segment size only changes file layout.

title: A backward-compatible Avro change
question: A topic's Avro schema is registered with BACKWARD compatibility, meaning consumers using the new schema must read data written with the previous schema. Which change is allowed?
options: Adding a new field without a default value
Adding a new field with a default value
Renaming an existing field without an alias
Changing a field's type from long to string
explanation: When a new-schema reader encounters old data missing a field, Avro fills in the default, so adding a field with a default is backward compatible. Without a default the reader has no value to use, incompatible type changes fail resolution, and renames without aliases look like a removed plus a new required field.

title: Stopping bad rows at write time
question: An upstream bug started sending negative quantities, which silently polluted a Delta Lake table used by dashboards. Which table-level feature would reject such writes?
options: Z-ordering the table by quantity
A CHECK constraint (e.g. quantity >= 0) that fails any transaction containing violating rows
Running VACUUM with a shorter retention period
Enabling the table's change data feed
explanation: Delta Lake CHECK constraints are validated on every write, and a transaction with violating rows fails, so bad data never becomes visible. Z-ordering is a layout optimisation, change data feed exposes row changes, and VACUUM deletes old files - none of them validate data.

title: Why Parquet speeds up analytics
question: A query reads 3 columns from a 200-column table and filters on a date. Why is Parquet typically much faster than CSV here?
options: It sorts every file by the primary key automatically
It is columnar, so only needed columns are read, and row-group statistics let readers skip data that cannot match the filter
It stores data uncompressed, so no decoding is needed
It keeps a B-tree index for every column
explanation: Parquet stores each column's values together, enabling column pruning and effective compression, and its metadata holds min/max statistics per row group for predicate pushdown. It is usually compressed, does not sort data automatically, and does not maintain B-tree indexes.

title: Thousands of tiny files
question: A streaming job writes a new Parquet file per partition every 30 seconds, producing millions of files of a few KB each. Queries over the table have become slow. What is the standard remedy?
options: Periodically compact small files into larger ones (e.g. Delta OPTIMIZE or Iceberg rewrite) and use larger write batches
Add more partition columns to spread the files further
Convert the files to JSON so they can be appended in place
Disable compression to make each file faster to open
explanation: Each file adds listing, open and metadata overhead, and tiny files compress poorly, so many small files hurt performance. Compaction rewrites them into appropriately large files, and longer triggers reduce creation of new ones. More partition columns create even more small files, and JSON or disabling compression worsens scans.

title: Partitioning by user_id
question: An events table in a data lake is partitioned by user_id (millions of users). Queries usually filter by date range, and query planning is now extremely slow. What is the better layout?
options: Partition by a random hash so files are evenly sized
Remove all partitioning and rely on full scans
Partition by both user_id and event timestamp to the second
Partition by a low-cardinality column matching common filters (e.g. event date) and cluster/sort by user_id within partitions
explanation: Partition columns should be low to moderate cardinality and align with frequent filters; millions of partitions create huge metadata overhead and tiny files. Date partitions prune effectively for range queries, and clustering by user_id still helps user lookups. Finer partitions worsen the problem, while full scans or random partitions remove pruning.

title: A new DAG creates hundreds of runs
question: A new Airflow DAG has a daily schedule, start_date set to one year ago and catchup=True. As soon as it is unpaused, the scheduler creates hundreds of DAG runs. Why?
options: Airflow retries the first run once per day of the start_date offset
The scheduler duplicates runs when the DAG file is parsed
Daily schedules always backfill exactly one year by default
Catchup schedules a run for every missed data interval between start_date and now
explanation: With catchup enabled, the scheduler creates DAG runs for every interval since start_date that has not run yet. Set catchup=False (the default in recent Airflow versions) or a recent start_date, and use explicit backfills when history is needed. Retries and file parsing do not create new DAG runs.

title: Passing a large DataFrame between tasks
question: A task pushes a 2 GB DataFrame to XCom so the next task can use it, and the metadata database is struggling. What is the recommended pattern?
options: Merge all tasks into one so XCom is not needed
Pickle the DataFrame to shrink it before pushing to XCom
Increase the metadata database's disk size
Write the data to external storage (e.g. object storage) and pass only a reference such as its path via XCom
explanation: XComs are meant for small pieces of metadata; by default they live in the Airflow metadata database. Large data should go to external storage, with tasks exchanging only references, or use a custom XCom backend. Bigger disks and pickling do not fix the misuse, and merging tasks loses retries and observability.

title: Slow scheduler from DAG files
question: DAG files query a database at module level to build a list of tables, and the scheduler's DAG parsing becomes slow and puts load on that database. What does Airflow best practice recommend?
options: Put the database query inside a try/except block
Combine all DAGs into a single file so it is parsed once
Avoid expensive top-level code; move such work into tasks or templated/runtime logic, since files are parsed repeatedly
Increase the DAG file processing interval to once per week
explanation: The DAG processor re-parses DAG files frequently, so any top-level code runs on every parse, slowing scheduling and hammering external systems. Expensive work belongs inside tasks executed at runtime. Rarely parsing delays picking up changes, try/except does not reduce cost, and one giant file is slower to parse.
